sourceRecords.sermonTitle: The Impact of the Gospel In Relationships Pt. 11
The Impact of the Gospel In Relationships Pt. 12

entries.title: Acts 2: The Spirit and a Believing Community
entries.commentary:
Acts 2 begins with God's promise being fulfilled. Jesus had told His disciples that the Holy Spirit would empower them to be witnesses, and at Pentecost people from different places heard the mighty works of God in their own languages. Peter stood and preached Jesus Christ, His death, resurrection, and exaltation. The response that followed was not the result of a personality-driven movement. God was drawing people to the gospel, and the apostles pointed them to Christ.

We need that same center in our churches today. The church is not built on a pastor's personality, a favorite ministry, or our ability to make everything look like the earliest days in Jerusalem. Those first believers devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, and prayer. They were joined together around Christ and His Word. Churches will face real disagreements and growing pains, just as the New Testament churches did, but we must not lose sight of the Savior, His mission, and our responsibility to one another.

entries.title: Receiving the Word, Baptism, and Belonging
entries.commentary: This helps us understand why salvation and believers' baptism is the pattern of belonging to the church. We are saved by Jesus Christ, not by signing a church membership card. Baptism is the believer's public act of obedience and identification with Christ. Immersion vividly pictures our burial with Christ and our rising to walk in newness of life. Acts 2:41 gives the order of receiving the word, being baptized, and being added; it does not describe the exact procedure for every baptism.

referenceTargets.rationale: Those added to the community share teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread and prayers
Acts 6 displays a maturing and organized community with internal responsibility

entries.title: Servants Chosen from Among the Church
entries.commentary:
The church in Acts 6 was growing, but growth brought a real problem. Some widows were being overlooked in the daily distribution, and the apostles did not pretend the complaint was unimportant. They called the disciples together and directed them to select trustworthy men from among themselves, men known for good reputation, wisdom, and the Spirit's fullness. The church had people who could be recognized, entrusted with responsibility, and called to serve.

Notice what this teaches us about leadership. We should not build the church around a personality, including the pastor's personality. Christ is the head of the church. Faithful leadership comes from a body of believers who know one another, recognize trustworthy servants, and take shared responsibility seriously. The apostles also protected their calling to prayer and the ministry of the Word while making sure practical care was not neglected.

Acts 6 does not hand every congregation a complete modern voting policy or membership form. It does give us a living picture of a church responding to needs through accountable, qualified service from within its fellowship. Our structures ought to support that biblical work. The goal is not simply to have leaders on paper; it is to be a church that cares for people in Christ's name.

referenceTargets.rationale: Recognized internal service and the equipping of all believers reinforce one another

entries.title: Pastoral Watchfulness and a Recognizable Flock
entries.commentary:
Hebrews 13:17 calls believers to respond faithfully to those who lead them, because those leaders watch over souls and will give an account. This is a massive responsibility. A pastor cannot faithfully shepherd an undefined crowd in the same personal way he shepherds the people entrusted to his care. The passage calls for both responsible leadership and a congregation willing to receive biblical guidance.

This is not permission to ignore people outside the church. Of course we should answer questions, offer help in a crisis, and share Jesus. However we must not neglect the flock we have been called to feed and lead.

Membership gives practical clarity to that relationship. It helps a congregation and its leaders know who is committed to walking together, receiving care, and bearing responsibility. Our ultimate Shepherd is Jesus Christ. Every pastor serves under Him, and no leader's authority can replace the authority of His Word.

referenceTargets.rationale: Leaders answer for pastoral watchfulness and equip believers for service

entries.title: Every Part Serving as the Body Grows
entries.commentary:
Ephesians 4 shows us that Christ gives leaders to equip His people for the work of ministry. The goal is not that a few people do all the work while everyone else watches. The whole body is to grow toward maturity, unity in the faith, and the knowledge of the Son of God. Christ is the head, and every part has a meaningful contribution as we speak the truth in love.

Our local church is one of the places where those responsibilities become concrete. We know people we can encourage, teach, strengthen, warn when necessary, and serve with the gifts God has given us. A congregation that learns to care for its own members is better prepared to care for its neighbors and share the gospel beyond its doors. The most outward-focused churches must take inward service seriously, because the life we share is part of our witness.

So where are we serving? We do not want to be satisfied with merely sitting and watching. We want to be servants. But the point is more than filling a volunteer schedule. As every part works properly under Christ, the body builds itself up in love.

referenceTargets.rationale: The broader body-of-Christ purpose explains why role-specific service matters

entries.title: Accountability Begins within the Church
entries.commentary:
Paul confronted the Corinthian church because serious, known sin was being tolerated among people who claimed to belong to the congregation. Rather than mourn and address it, the church had become proud. Paul drew a clear distinction between the church's responsibility toward those within its fellowship and God's judgment of those outside. He was not commissioning believers to police every stranger in the community. He was calling the church to take its own holiness and witness seriously.

We can spend so much time talking about the sin of the world while refusing to face sin we know about in our own congregations. That is neither love nor faithfulness. Belonging to a church means we are willing to care enough to speak truth, to be corrected ourselves, and to seek the spiritual good of our brothers and sisters. A recognizable body of believers makes this mutual responsibility possible.

This passage does not authorize rumors, private investigations, or people looking for someone to condemn. Paul's case concerns grave misconduct the church already knew about, and any corrective action must be handled biblically and responsibly. We must join this passage with the call to gentleness and restoration in Galatians 6:1. The aim is a holy, faithful church, not a congregation ruled by suspicion.

referenceTargets.rationale: Church discipline must not be presented as permission for harsh judgment; restoration is gentle and self-aware

entries.title: Restoration with Gentleness and Humility
entries.commentary:
Galatians 6 reminds us how to respond when a brother or sister is caught in a trespass. Those who are walking by the Spirit are to restore that person in a spirit of gentleness, watching themselves because they too can be tempted. The next verse calls us to bear one another's burdens. There is no room here for pride, cruelty, or delight in somebody else's failure.

Accountability in the church is not a call to go looking for people to expose. We all need the Lord's grace, and any one of us can stumble. When someone needs correction, our hearts should be set on helping that person return to faithful fellowship with Christ and His people. Love does not pretend sin is harmless, but neither does it forget the person who needs care.

This is one of the reasons local belonging is precious. We are not meant to be disconnected believers who face every spiritual battle alone. In the church, we can encourage, warn, carry burdens, confess our own need for help, and restore one another gently. That is accountability shaped by the Spirit rather than by pride.

referenceTargets.rationale: Restoration and humility are essential when applying congregational correction

entries.title: Romans: The Gospel That Changes Our Lives
entries.commentary:
If we want to understand the gospel and the salvation God gives us through Jesus Christ, Romans is a place to dig deeply. Paul begins by declaring that he is not ashamed of the gospel because it is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes. From there he shows us that God judges without partiality, that all of us have sinned, and that we cannot make ourselves righteous by our own works. Abraham believed God, and righteousness was credited to him by faith. Through Jesus Christ we are justified by faith and have peace with God.

But the good news does not end with forgiveness. In Christ we have died to sin and are called to walk in newness of life. We belong to the risen Savior, and God’s purpose and love give His people confidence even when life is difficult. Paul also deals seriously with Israel, election, and the mercy and wisdom of God, until we arrive at his great declaration of praise at the end of chapter 11. We cannot exhaust the riches of God by reducing Romans to a few favorite verses.

This is why we study the gospel before talking about how to live. Romans does not teach us to earn salvation by becoming better people. It shows us what God has done through Christ, and then calls us to live as people who have received His mercy. The gospel that saves us must also shape the way we treat one another.

entries.title: Romans 12: Mercy, Renewal, and a Changed Life
entries.commentary:
When Paul urges us to present our bodies as living sacrifices, he appeals to the mercies of God. That order matters. We do not change our lives so that God might save us. We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, and when God saves us, He changes us. Romans 12 is the outworking of the gospel that Romans 1–11 has been explaining.

The miracle of salvation reaches far deeper than a cleaned-up reputation. We were dead in trespasses and sins, but God makes us alive in Christ. He forgives, frees us from bondage to sin, gives us His Spirit, and keeps His people by His power. Change is not the entrance requirement for salvation; it is a necessary fruit of what God has done. As we keep walking with Christ, our thoughts, actions, and ambitions ought to be brought increasingly into line with His Word. That is not legalism. It is the life of a person being transformed.

God has also given us a shared work. Our gifts and responsibilities may look different, but our purpose is the same: to glorify Him. Each part of the church matters, and we ought to ask whether our service contributes to its harmony or adds conflict that does not need to be there.

That change must become visible, including in our relationships. It is a painful thing when someone who has spent time around us is surprised to discover that we follow Jesus. Our witness should not depend on a church building, a religious label, or what we post online. People should see Christ’s work in how we speak and respond. A renewed mind does not simply ask, “What am I entitled to do?” It asks, “What honors God, and what will show others the gospel?”

referenceTargets.rationale: God’s mercy and renewed mind ground living response rather than retaliation.

entries.title: Romans 12:17: Refuse Retaliation, Pursue What Is Honorable
entries.commentary:
Romans 12:17 calls us to do two things that our flesh often resists. We must not repay anyone evil for evil, and we must take care to do what is right in the sight of others. When someone wrongs us, it can feel natural to give them the same treatment in return. We may even try to dress that response up in biblical language. But being hurt does not give us permission to be hateful, petty, or cruel.

Sometimes we reach for the Old Testament statement about an eye for an eye as though it gives us a personal right to get even. That instruction belonged to a setting of lawful judgment; it was not a private revenge permit. And the Old Testament itself warns us not to say we will repay evil or do to someone exactly as they have done to us. This does not mean Christians have no lawful rights, must ignore crimes, or must become doormats. There is a difference between proper legal process and allowing resentment to take over our own actions. We cross a line when we decide that another person's wrong justifies our own sin.

Scripture gives us living examples of this choice. Joseph had the authority to punish the brothers who sold him, yet he considered what was right and used his position to preserve their lives, recognizing God's hand in his circumstances. David could have killed Saul in the cave, but he listened to his conscience, respected what was right before the Lord, and restrained his men from attacking. Stephen, even as he was being stoned, prayed for his attackers rather than calling for their destruction. None of these examples makes the evil done to them acceptable. They remind us that another person's wrongdoing never gives us permission to stop obeying God.

I know how quickly a sarcastic response can become a fleshly reaction. The Lord does not excuse it merely because I can get a laugh. In the same way, angry public talk, threats, and contempt toward people we disagree with do not somehow become righteous because we believe our cause is right. We cannot allow the circumstances around us to dictate whether we obey God's Word.

Paul also tells us to consider what is honorable before everyone. The word translated “respect” carries the sense of giving thought or care to something. Our conduct requires that kind of attention. We do not allow unbelievers to decide what God's Word means, but we must care whether the life they see in us points toward Jesus or drives them away. The church is called to minister, not merely to win arguments. When people are hungry, our responsibility to love and serve them does not disappear because we have a strong opinion about what government should do.

Ask yourself how easily you take matters into your own hands, and how readily you carry an old wound into a new relationship. Grudges damage the fellowship of believers. We ought not let personal hurt overcome our love for brothers and sisters in Christ. Following Jesus in a world that resists Him can be costly. Yet our calling remains to show His holiness and goodness, not to be overcome by evil. Paul continues the argument through peace, leaving vengeance to God, caring for enemies, and overcoming evil with good; those next instructions grow out of the same gospel-shaped response.

referenceTargets.rationale: Proverbs warns against personal repaying of evil and waiting on the Lord; Jake reads it to ground Romans 12:17.
Both passages reject saying I will do to him as he has done to me; cited in the sermon.
Differentiate civic judicial restitution in Mosaic law from a believer privately taking revenge.
Concern for honorable conduct before God and before people is a shared ethical expression.
Explicitly prohibits repaying evil for evil and directs believers to pursue good for all.
Read as immediate surrounding exhortation to blessing, sympathy and humble treatment of others.
Verses 18-21 complete the unit with peace, divine vengeance, enemy care and doing good, read aloud but deferred in detailed exposition.

entries.title: Romans 12:18: Peace without Surrendering the Truth
entries.commentary:
Paul's instruction is clear: if it is possible, as far as it depends on us, we are to live at peace with everyone. We cannot control another person's heart, attitudes, or choices. That is why Paul says "if possible." But those words are not an excuse for being difficult, combative, or careless with people. As far as the responsibility belongs to us, we should be a people who pursue peace. If there is no peace, may it not be because we were the ones determined to create conflict.

This command comes right after Paul's charge not to repay evil for evil. When somebody wrongs us, it doesn't suddenly become right for us to do wrong back. The rest of the passage tells us not to take private revenge and to answer the needs of an enemy with good. The gospel changes what we do when someone treats us badly. We have to consider what is right before God, not merely what would feel satisfying in the moment.

At the same time, peace does not mean surrendering what God has spoken. There will be occasions when another person refuses peace because of our allegiance to Jesus Christ. We do not have to deny the truth of the gospel to avoid disagreement. But standing firm in truth and treating people with hatred are not the same thing. Religious violence and hostility are not the mission Christ has given His church. We are called to love people, show compassion, and speak the good news to our neighbors, including people who do not share our faith. Their greatest need is the same need we had: Jesus Christ.

Now bring the verse home. Where are we causing needless tension in a family, a friendship, a workplace, or a church? Are we too comfortable living in conflict? Think about a group of musicians playing distinct parts of one piece. Their instruments and responsibilities are different, yet they work together in harmony. God has given His people different gifts and forms of service, but our shared purpose is to glorify Him. This is not a demand that everybody be identical; it is a reminder that each of us must do our part faithfully. So ask yourself the question Paul places before us: as much as it depends on me, am I a source of peace or a source of conflict?

referenceTargets.rationale: Part of one nonretaliation and peacemaking argument; v.17 frames v.18
Private revenge is refused while active good toward the enemy is commanded
Earlier exhortations to bless persecutors and practice humility inform “with all people”

entries.title: Genesis 45:1–8: Joseph Chooses Preservation over Revenge
entries.commentary:
Joseph had every human reason to be angry with his brothers. They had hated him, sold him, and caused suffering that he could not simply undo. Now, when they came before him needing food, the balance of power was completely different. Joseph held a position in Egypt from which he could have used his authority against them. Instead, the passage shows his tears, his willingness to identify himself to them, and his concern to preserve life.

Joseph did not pretend his brothers' actions were harmless. He named what they had done. But he also saw that God had worked through those painful years to preserve his family during a famine. His brothers' evil intentions did not become righteous because God accomplished something good. Rather, Joseph refused to allow their wrongdoing to set the standard for his response. He considered what was right before the Lord.

When we are wronged, revenge can seem almost natural. We rehearse what was done to us, and we imagine what we might do if the opportunity came. Joseph's example presses us in another direction. Will we use whatever influence or opportunity we have to wound somebody back, or can we respond with mercy and seek what truly brings life? God can be at work in circumstances we would never have chosen. Our calling is not to repay evil with evil but to do what is right.

referenceTargets.rationale: Joseph’s treatment of brothers demonstrates good rather than revenge, in narrative context

entries.title: 1 Samuel 24:3–7: David Refuses an Easy Revenge
entries.commentary:
David was fleeing from Saul, who had pursued him and sought his life. Then Saul entered the very cave where David and his men were hiding. Humanly speaking, the opportunity could hardly have been more convenient. David's men urged him to act, and it would have been easy to tell himself that removing Saul was the quickest way out of danger.

Yet David's conscience troubled him even after he cut a piece from Saul's robe. Saul's wrongdoing did not erase the fact that he was the Lord's anointed king. David refused to stretch out his hand against him, and he restrained the men who were ready to follow a different path. An open door is not automatically a command from God. We must ask not only what we can do but what is right in God's sight.

This is where our own hearts need examination. Someone can treat us unjustly, and we may have the perfect chance to embarrass them, punish them, or give them what they gave us. But the fact that vengeance is within reach does not make it obedience. David could have returned evil for evil. Instead, he chose restraint. We should be governed by God's Word rather than by our anger, pride, or a crowd encouraging us to strike back.

referenceTargets.rationale: David refuses to exploit a chance to injure Saul and restrains his companions

entries.title: 1 Samuel 24:16–19: Good Answers a Wrongdoer
entries.commentary:
When David finally spoke to Saul, Saul himself had to acknowledge the difference between his own wicked treatment of David and David's good treatment of him. Saul recognized that David had an opportunity to kill him and had let him leave safely. The one who had been pursuing David was now confronted with the righteousness of the man he had wronged.

I want us to see the effect of that decision. David's men watched a leader refuse revenge when revenge was available. Saul heard a testimony that exposed his own behavior without David having to murder him. That does not mean Saul's tears guarantee that every conflict was permanently healed. It does mean the choice to do what is right can speak more powerfully than striking back.

When we are tempted to justify retaliation, consider the witness we bear. We may not get an apology, and the other person may not change. But we can still make the righteous choice entrusted to us. Doing good is not the same as declaring evil acceptable. It is choosing not to become the wrongdoer ourselves.

referenceTargets.rationale: Saul’s words confirm David’s righteous restraint later in the same chapter

entries.title: Acts 7:54–60: Stephen Prays While Being Stoned
entries.commentary:
Stephen was not facing a mild disagreement. His opponents were enraged by his witness, drove him out, and stoned him. Even as they killed him, Stephen called upon the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and asked that their sin not be held against them. He did not answer their hatred with his own curse.

That kind of response forces us to examine how we react to much smaller injuries. We can carry bitterness over a careless remark or decide to get even over a slight. Stephen was suffering violence for his testimony about Christ, yet his last prayer sought mercy for those hurting him. The power of the gospel is seen in a heart that can pray while being wronged.

There is a beautiful connection here to the Lord Jesus. At the cross, Jesus prayed for forgiveness as He suffered. Later, Stephen followed that example. We should never imagine the Christian life means pretending persecution and wrongdoing are good. Rather, we see a servant of Christ who trusted his Lord, bore witness faithfully, and refused to surrender his heart to revenge. This is the kind of Christlike response Paul's words in Romans 12 call us to pursue.

referenceTargets.rationale: Stephen’s response under violence resembles Jesus and embodies nonretaliation
Stephen asks mercy for his killers after Jesus’ crucifixion prayer; parallel is thematic, not chronological prophecy

entries.title: Luke 23:34: Christ Prays for His Enemies
entries.commentary:
At Calvary we see more than an example of patience. We see the Savior suffering at the hands of sinful people and, praying for those responsible. If anyone had authority to call down judgment on His enemies, it was Jesus Christ. Yet He did not answer the cruelty of the cross with personal retaliation.

We have to remember who was hanging there. Jesus did not come simply to teach us to be nicer to difficult people. He gave Himself for sinners. His suffering and sacrifice are the foundation of the forgiveness we need, because apart from Him we were the ones in need of mercy. What He accomplished at the cross makes the gospel the good news we carry to people who may even oppose us.

When I am tempted to repay evil for evil, the cross calls me to look again at the Lord's mercy. His prayer does not tell us that cruelty is righteous or that justice does not matter. It shows a Savior who can offer forgiveness in the midst of hatred. We are not Christ, and we cannot save anybody by our suffering, but because we belong to Him, we can respond with compassion and point people toward the forgiveness He offers.
